title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context (§§40–43 of E420): Euler varies the curve y(x) behind the functional ∫Z dx, with Z = Z(x,y,p,q,…), p = dy/dx and dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + … . The comparison curves need not end at the same point. Their endpoints may lie anywhere on a straight line Mω through the endpoint M, making an angle ω with the curve. The boundary (second) part of the variation is proportional to Z + [(1+p²) tan ω/(1 − p tan ω)]·(P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² − …). It vanishes when tan ω = Z/(pZ − (1+p²)(P − dQ/dx + …)). This is the transversality condition for an endpoint sliding on a curve with slope φ': Z + (φ' − p)·P = 0, written through the angle. Euler singles out the case where the transversal line is normal to the extremal (ω = 90°, tan ω = ∞). The denominator must then vanish: pZ = (1+p²)(P − dQ/dx + …).

On this page (§43) he asks which integrands Z have this property identically. He assumes Z depends only on x, y, p (so Q = R = 0). The condition becomes the first-order equation pZ = (1+p²)∂Z/∂p in the single variable p, with x and y frozen as parameters. Separating gives dZ/Z = p dp/(1+p²), hence ln Z = ln√(1+p²) + ln C, where C is an arbitrary function V(x,y). So Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²) and the functional is ∫V ds. He interprets this physically: if a body moves along the curve with speed 1/V(x,y), then V ds is the element of time, and ∫V ds is the travel time from A to M (completed on p.62).

Modern statement: for a first-order Lagrangian F(x,y,y'), transversality coincides with orthogonality for every curve and every point if and only if F = n(x,y)√(1+y'²). These are the isotropic, Fermat-type (conformally Euclidean) metrics, i.e. travel time in an isotropic medium.
errors: No mathematical error. The derivation is correct, including treating V(x,y) as the 'constant' of integration in the p-equation.
Minor gap: the case Z > 0 is implicitly assumed when taking logarithms; Z ≡ 0 is a trivial further solution.
The 'only if' direction is proved only for Z without q, r, …; the higher-order case is announced by the general equation but not solved.

ideas.what: Condition for the free-endpoint (sliding-on-a-line) boundary term to vanish, expressed via the angle ω between the transversal and the extremal
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange (variable endpoint problems); the name 'transversality' is due to Kneser (1900)
ideas.where_published: E420 itself; variable-endpoint problems also in Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385) and the 1771 variational papers

ideas.what: Characterization: transversality equals orthogonality iff Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²), obtained by solving pZ = (1+p²)Z_p
ideas.modern_name: transversality reduces to orthogonality exactly for functionals ∫n(x,y)ds (isotropic / conformally flat metric)
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard textbook fact (e.g. Gelfand–Fomin, Bolza); usually not attributed to anyone, and its connection to Euler is rarely mentioned

ideas.what: Interpretation of ∫V ds as travel time with speed 1/V(x,y)
ideas.modern_name: Fermat's principle / optical length; brachistochrone-type functionals
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744), brachistochrone in resisting/general media

missed.claim: Euler identifies, as a necessary and sufficient criterion, the class of integrands for which transversals are normals: precisely travel-time (optical) functionals ∫V ds. This implicitly generalizes Johann Bernoulli's observation that synchronous curves cut the cycloids orthogonally. It anticipates the orthogonality of wavefronts and rays in isotropic media (Malus–Dupin, Hamilton) and Kneser's theory of transversals and geodesic parallels. Euler does not draw the wavefront/field consequence, and histories rarely credit him with the 'iff' characterization.
missed.quote: Hic casus prae caeteris omnino notatu dignus ... quo recta Mω sit ad curuam principalem in puncto M normalis ... Z=V√(1+pp) ... per tempus, quo corpus quodpiam per curuam AM promouetur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical-priority point. The textbook fact that transversality reduces to orthogonality exactly for isotropic (Fermat) Lagrangians is stated here in 1772 with proof. The fact itself is well known.

missed.claim: Euler sets up the normal-transversal condition for higher-order integrands, pZ = (1+p²)(P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² − …), but immediately restricts to Q = R = 0. Characterizing higher-order Lagrangians with this property is left open.
missed.quote: Sumamus autem praeterea in Z non ingredi litteras q, r etc. ita vt sit Q=0, R=0
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of minor interest only. It is a straightforward but untreated generalization, and the condition then becomes a differential condition along the extremal rather than an identity.

deep.surprise_reason: The result itself (transversality = orthogonality iff F = n(x,y)√(1+y'²)) is standard textbook material. What is noteworthy is that Euler states and proves the characterization explicitly in 1772 and ties it to travel time, a priority not usually emphasized. It is a modest historical credit, not a new mathematical result.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors. '√' is rendered as \surd in the transcription and as V-like radical signs in the print; the formulas read Z = V√(1+pp) and ∫V dx√(1+pp) as transcribed.
In 'L.Z = L.√(1+pp) + L.C quae constans functio quaecunque...', the relative 'quae' refers to the constant C; the transcription is faithful to the print.
